title: Numeric For Loops
summary: `for i = start, finish, step do ... end` counts from start to finish (inclusive) with an optional step. The loop variable is local and read-only.

syntax: for i = 1, 10 do          -- i: 1,2,...,10 (step defaults to 1)
for i = 0, 1, 0.25 do     -- fractional steps work

details.heading: Bounds are evaluated once
details.body: start, finish and step are computed once before the loop begins. Changing related variables inside the loop does not change the endpoint.

details.heading: The loop variable is read-only
details.body: Assigning to `i` inside the body is an error in Luau. If you need a moving counter, use a separate local.

explanation.whatItIs: The counting loop. 'Do this N times', 'count down from 10', 'hit every third index'.
explanation.whyItExists: Counting is the most common loop shape; a dedicated syntax keeps it short and off-by-error-free.
whenToUse: Stepping through indices with a custom step
whenNotToUse: For iterating over a table's elements — use generic for (`for i, v in t`); it survives length changes and reads better
When the endpoint changes during the loop — numeric for locks bounds at start
explanation.mentalModel:
```text
for i = 1, 3 do
    print(i)
end
--> 1
--> 2
--> 3     (finish is INCLUSIVE)

for i = 1, 0 do   -- start already past finish
end               --> runs zero times
```
tips: Inclusive upper bound trips people up: `for i = 1, #list` visits exactly #list elements — perfect for arrays
Negative step needs start > finish or the loop never runs

The loop variable is fresh each iteration — safe to close over in callbacks? No! It's shared per-iteration; capture with `local j = i` if needed (Luau: loop vars are per-iteration, so closures actually get their own copy — this is a Luau improvement over Lua 5.1)
commonMistakes: Expecting the finish to be exclusive (like Python's range) — it's inclusive
Trying to reassign `i` inside the body — that's an error
Writing `for i = #t, 1` without `-1` and getting zero iterations

examples.title: Countdown + backwards removal
examples.code:
-- Classic countdown
for t = 5, 1, -1 do
    print(t)
    task.wait(1)
end
print("GO!")

-- Safe removal while iterating (backwards!)
local items = {"keep", "drop", "keep", "drop"}
for i = #items, 1, -1 do
    if items[i] == "drop" then
        table.remove(items, i)
    end
end
examples.whyItWorks: Walking backwards means removing item i never shifts the items you still need to visit (1..i-1).

examples.title: Spawning a grid of parts
examples.code:
for x = -2, 2 do
    for z = -2, 2 do
        local part = Instance.new("Part")
        part.Size = Vector3.new(1, 1, 1)
        part.Position = Vector3.new(x * 4, 0.5, z * 4)
        part.Parent = workspace
    end
end
-- 25 parts in a 5x5 grid
